title: The humble plea
hookLine: the Lord's humble servants ask the True Guru for the Name (Gujri M4, ang 10)
last: YOUR CHANCE — NOW IS THE CHANCE.

lines: A GURU'S SHABAD THAT ONLY ASKS.
cards: Some people find it easy to ask for help. Others would rather drive around lost for an hour than ask for directions. They say I'm fine, I've got it, don't worry about me, and then carry it alone.
Asking can feel like admitting you're small. Guru Ram Das, a Guru the sangat bowed to, wrote a shabad that is nothing but asking, and calls himself very small indeed.

teach.h: TWO GUJRI SHABADS, BEFORE SO PURAKH.
teach.b: In Rehras, after the three shabads we heard a few days ago, come two more in Raag Gujri, before the So Purakh group. We're going back for them now. The first is by Guru Ram Das.
It begins, in paraphrase: O servant of the Lord, True Guru, True Being, I make my plea to the Guru.

teach.h: WE ARE WORMS AND INSECTS; WE SEEK SHELTER.
teach.b: We are worms and insects, True Guru, and we seek Your shelter. Be kind, and let the light of the Name shine. Worms and insects.
Guru Ram Das was the fourth Guru, remembered in Sikh tradition as the founder of the town that grew into Amritsar. And here he speaks as the smallest of creatures, asking.
Then the refrain: my friend, divine Guru, light up the Lord's Name in me. And then a line you'll recognize.

teach.h: THE LORD'S PRAISE IS MY RAHRAAS.
teach.b: Through the Guru's teaching, the Name is the friend of my breath, and the Lord's praise is my rahraas: the very word the evening prayer is named for, provisions for the road.
The shabad goes on: great is the fortune of the Lord's servants who have faith in Him and thirst for Him. So this is what a plea looks like in Sikh prayer. Not bargaining, not a list of demands.
An honest admission of smallness, and a request for the one thing that matters: the Name.

teach.h: BINAU: A HUMBLE PETITION FOR THE NAME.
teach.b: The word for it here is binau, a humble petition. It's the same spirit as Ardas, where Sikhs stand and ask, with folded hands.

how: Har ke jan satgur satpurkhaa is the fourth shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; its line naming the Lord's praise as rahraas is often given as the source of the prayer's name.

o: a vow of silence kept before prayer
a humble plea, asked with folded hands
a list of demands brought to God

games.q: the humble plea — tap the pairs.
p: the fourth Guru, the voice of this shabad

s: the word rahraas appears inside this shabad
the Lord's praise is my rahraas, my provisions.
in this shabad the Guru asks for wealth and success
he asks for one thing: the light of the Name.
in Rehras this shabad comes before the So Purakh group
it's the fourth shabad; we stepped back to hear it.

games.q: a Guru the sangat bows to writes a plea to the True Guru. how does he describe himself?
o: as a great teacher with much to offer.
as a worm, an insect, seeking shelter.
as an equal making a deal.
games.why: Guru Ram Das writes: we are worms and insects, we seek Your shelter; be kind and light up the Name.

practice: Think of something you've been carrying alone, and of who could help: a friend, a sibling, a colleague, a doctor. If you pray, bring it to God first, in the plain words of your own heart, or say Waheguru once.
Then picture asking, simply, could you help me with this, and notice what it feels like in your chest, and breathe through it.

wordCard.voice: Binau, a humble plea: Guru Ram Das asks the True Guru for the light of the Name. This week: hearsay, remembering, that Being, the true Creator, the muddy pool, your chance, and now the humble ask.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: binau, a humble plea; binau karau gur paas, I make my plea to the Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: the humble ask. In this shabad, the asking is the prayer. A week, done.
